display.purpose: Rare. A hub front page or an app's own landing header. A working surface does not have one.

title.purpose: The name of the surface, and section headings. The largest type on a normal screen.

body.purpose: Answers and prose — anything written in sentences by a person or a model.

dense.purpose: The workhorse row: step summaries, list items, secondary controls. Most of the interface.

mono.purpose: Commands, paths, shell output, diffs, table cells, IDs, counts, elapsed times. Always tabular figures.

label.purpose: Panel headings, table column headers, mode chips, metadata. Uppercase and tracked so it reads as a classification.

micro.purpose: Rail captions and sub-labels where the word only disambiguates an icon.

shadows.name: armed-edge
shadows.purpose: This control has content and is ready to fire. Paired with a border mixed 32% toward brand.

shadows.name: hearing-edge
shadows.purpose: This control is currently taking dictation.

shadows.name: selected-edge
shadows.purpose: The incumbent selected-nav-item and selected-table-row marker the armed edge is derived from.

shadows.name: none
shadows.purpose: The default, and the rule. Depth is tonal; there is no drop shadow in the component layer.

motion.name: nj-ease
motion.purpose: The only easing curve. Exponential ease-out: fast departure, long settle.

motion.name: nj-fast
motion.purpose: State transitions — border, background, colour, icon rotation.

motion.name: nj-slow
motion.purpose: Arrival. A step row settling into the ledger.

motion.name: nj-step-in
motion.value: @keyframes nj-step-in { from { transform: translateY(-3px); opacity: 0.55; } to { transform: none; opacity: 1; } }
motion.purpose: New content arrives already visible and travels the last few pixels. Fading up from zero is the spinner's grammar.

motion.name: nj-pulse
motion.purpose: A live or waiting indicator. Opacity only, so it composites.

motion.name: wave-tick
motion.purpose: A per-frame level meter. Scales one fixed height; never resizes the element.

narrative.overview:
This is a dark room with an instrument in it. The canvas is near-black (#0a0b0f) and almost nothing on it is coloured — panels are separated from the canvas by two or three points of lightness and a one-pixel hairline, never by a shadow and never by a card. Colour does not decorate here; it reports. When something on this surface goes indigo, green, amber or red, a machine is telling you its state, and that is the only reason those hues ever appear.

The register is dense and factual. The whole working type ramp lives between 9.5px and 14px, and the single largest thing on a typical screen is a 14px semibold word. That is not an accident of scale — it is the product's stated position: the one person who uses this reads fast, knows the domain, and would rather see forty real values than eight pretty cards. Monospace carries the other half of the argument. Every command, path, ref, count and elapsed time is set in JetBrains Mono with tabular figures, so a column of numbers can be compared by eye instead of re-measured; prose is set in the system sans so the two never get confused for one another.

The world rejects two things by name. It rejects the card grid as a way of browsing — that was tried once in the AI Rankings app and had to be rebuilt as a table. And it rejects depth-as-rank: there is not one shadow utility in the entire component layer, because a raised surface implies an importance the data has not earned. Depth is tonal (canvas → panel → panel-2 → elevated) and boundaries are hairlines.
keyCharacteristics: Near-black canvas with four tonal surface steps, separated by 1px hairlines
A working type ramp that tops out at 14px; display type is exceptional, not structural
Monospace with tabular figures for every machine fact; sans for every human sentence
One indigo for what is armed or current; green/amber/red strictly for state
Flat by construction — no drop shadows in the component layer
Tables and bordered strips over cards and grids

rules.name: The State-Only Rule
rules.body: Green, amber and red are reserved for machine state — reachable, waiting on you, failed. If a hue is being chosen because it looks good next to the one beside it, the wrong palette is open. Neutrals and one indigo carry everything else.

rules.name: The Darker-On-Hover Rule
rules.body: A filled control's hover state is derived from its rest colour by mixing toward black, never by stepping to the lighter sibling. Moving brand-2 to brand on hover relocates a contrast breach to the exact moment the pointer is on the control; brand-press removes it.

rules.name: The Ink Budget Rule
rules.body: ink is for the thing being read right now. If a screen has more than a handful of ink strings on it, the hierarchy has collapsed and everything is shouting — demote the rest to ink-muted.

rules.name: The Reason-Not-A-Colour Rule
rules.body: A status indicator never carries meaning alone. Every dot is accompanied by a word, and every off state is accompanied by the reason it is off in a plain sentence. A red dot sends the owner to a log file; "the local agent is not running" sends them to the fix.

rules.name: The Machine Voice Rule
rules.body: If a string came out of a machine and a human would have to compare it to another string — a command, a path, a ref, a count, an elapsed time, a file size, a PID — it is monospace with tabular figures. If a human wrote it, it is sans. There is no third case.

rules.name: The Fourteen-Pixel Ceiling Rule
rules.body: On a working surface, 14px semibold is the top of the ramp. Reaching for 20px or 24px to signal importance is the card-grid instinct wearing different clothes; signal importance with position and colour instead.

rules.name: The Loaded-Not-Asked Rule
rules.body: Naming a font in a token does not load it. --font-mono asked for JetBrains Mono for a long time while every string on every machine quietly fell through to Consolas. A surface that names a face must load it (next/font) and bind it into the token, or the design's named voice is fiction.

rules.name: The Nothing-Scrolls-Away Rule
rules.body: Exactly one region scrolls. If a status, a capability list or the input itself can leave the screen, the arrangement has failed regardless of how it looks at rest.

rules.name: The Same-X Rule
rules.body: Every element in a column shares its left edge — the command line, each block, the empty state, the section headings. Centring one thing "because it's the empty state" makes it the only object on the surface that does not line up with the column it belongs to.

rules.name: The Flat-By-Construction Rule
rules.body: Surfaces never lift. If two things need separating, step the tone or draw a hairline; if something needs marking, light its edge from inside. A drop shadow in a new component is a bug, not a style choice.

rules.name: The Two-Hairlines Rule
rules.body: line for the edge of a thing, line-soft for the edges inside it. Never the reverse, and never two line borders adjacent.

rules.name: The No-Nesting Rule
rules.body: A bordered strip contains sections, not other strips. If content needs a second frame, give it a line-soft inset pane on canvas — a hole, not a tile.

rules.name: The Settle-Don't-Fade Rule
rules.body: New content enters at full opacity and travels the last few pixels. If it fades up from zero, it reads as a loading state even after it has loaded.

rules.name: The One-Curve Rule
rules.body: cubic-bezier(0.16, 1, 0.3, 1), 160ms or 220ms. A second easing curve on a surface is a second opinion about what kind of machine this is.

dos: Do take every colour from the @theme block in src/app/globals.css. It is the single source; a new hex in a component is a bug unless it is a documented state value.
Do set every command, path, ref, count, size and elapsed time in JetBrains Mono with tabular figures, and load the face rather than only naming it in a token.
Do separate surfaces by tone and a 1px hairline: line for a container's own edge, line-soft for everything inside it.
Do make hover on a filled control go darker, using color-mix(… , black) from the rest colour rather than a lighter sibling.
Do pair every status indicator with a word, and every off state with the specific reason it is off and the command that fixes it.
Do keep the whole working ramp between 9.5px and 14px, and reach for position, weight and colour before size.
Do declare :focus-visible once at a surface's root (2px brand, 2px offset) so every control is reachable and visible by keyboard.
Do let new content arrive at full opacity and settle, on the one curve, at 160 or 220ms — and disable it under prefers-reduced-motion.
Do render a machine result as what it is: a table as a table, a diff coloured per line, a picture as a picture.
Do pin the things that say where am I, what can I do and what is running, and scroll exactly one region.
donts: Don't add a drop shadow. There is not one in the component layer; depth is tonal. box-shadow is permitted only as the inset left-edge state marker.
Don't build a card grid to browse records. It was rejected once already and rebuilt as a table. Dense rows, real values, one screen.
Don't nest a bordered strip inside a bordered strip. Use a line-soft inset pane on canvas when content needs its own frame.
Don't use green, amber or red for anything that is not machine state, and don't use brand to make something look important rather than to mark it as armed or current.
Don't use ink for body text in bulk. Most text on a screen is ink-muted; ink is for the thing being read right now.
Don't let a focus ring and a state indicator wear the same appearance. Armed is a lit left edge; focus is the outline ring. Two meanings in one appearance means neither reads.
Don't print JSON at a person, and don't flatten a multi-step run into one sentence. The steps and their outputs are the product.
Don't introduce a second easing curve, a second radius scale, or a font size outside the ramp because one component "needs" it.
Don't animate height, width or top on anything that runs continuously — scale and translate a fixed box instead.
Don't copy the glows, pill radii or saturated pinks and cyans from the mcl-* and ds-* blocks in globals.css. Those are individual apps' local vocabularies, not this system.
